newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Burundi's Buyoya accuses OAU of hypocrisy on coups.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya accuses OAU of hypocrisy on coups.

text.p: Burundi military ruler Pierre Buyoya accused the Organisation of African Unity on Wednesday of double standards in condemning undemocratic governments and military coups, but living with them among its powerful members.

Addressing a news conference in Zimbabwe at the end of a three-day OAU summit, Buyoya, who seized power in a military coup last July, said however he supported the general thrust of the 53-member organisation towards democracy despite the apparent lack of consistency.
He said this before Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe and OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim called on both Burundi and Nigeria to return to democracy.
Mugabe, the new OAU chairman, told a news conference: "We are getting tougher and tougher each time. I can assure that for future coups, it will be much tougher."
Earlier, asked whether he felt that coups in small countries such as Burundi and Sierra Leone were unfairly targetted by the OAU for condemnation, sanctions and political pressure, Buyoya had said:

"OAU is a mature organisation, but we notice that in the implementation of certain principles, there are two ways of implementing these decisions, depending on whether one country is important, wealthy or not.
"What we would like to wish is that OAU principles be applied in the same way to everybody otherwise only small countries will be suffering while wealthy and big countries will be living pretty."

Nigeria's military government is leading military efforts by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to restore Sierra Leone President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah who was overthrown by junior military officers on May 25.

Asked whether he had been comfortable sitting through the three-day OAU summit at which several leaders, including U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, called for an end to coups and military rule on the continent, Buyoya replied:
"I was comfortable. I recognise the principle that there should be no coups d'etat, but I am not not prepared to see the country disintegrate in the name of democracy."

Buyoya said his government was moving towards democracy and called for the lifting of economic sanctions imposed on Burundi by neighbouring states to try to force him out of power after he ousted civilian Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya.

"We are still working on a programme, still negotiating and I don't know how long that will take," he said, adding that it was also premature to indicate whether he would contest any democracy elections in Burundi.
